text: DSH Monitor 是一个面向 web 客户端的系统监控插件，通过 DSH 侧栏提供机器、仓库、Kubernetes 和 macOS 应用面板。它汇总 CPU、内存、磁盘与进程状态，查看 Git 仓库和集群工作负载，并呈现应用信息与配置。适合在 DSH 中集中查看开发环境状态；安装后可按需设置仓库目录和 Kubernetes context。

DSH Monitor adds a System panel to the DSH web sidebar for machine metrics, Git repositories, Kubernetes health, and macOS application status. Use it to check your development environment from inside DSH, with optional repository and Kubernetes context settings.
想在 DSH 侧栏里看电脑的 CPU、内存和磁盘状态。
有没有办法集中查看我正在开发的 Git 仓库状态？
让 DSH 帮我汇总 Kubernetes 集群里的节点和工作负载健康情况。
想在 DSH 里检查 macOS 已安装应用和 Homebrew 更新。
Can I monitor my machine and project repositories from the DSH sidebar?
I need a dashboard for Kubernetes workloads and cluster health inside DSH.
DSH Monitor 的功能「机器状态面板」：在系统面板汇总 CPU、内存、磁盘、负载、电池和进程信息，并根据配置阈值标示告警。打开侧栏中的系统面板即可查看当前采集结果。
DSH Monitor 的功能「Kubernetes 集群概览」：通过 kubectl 读取集群对象，并将节点、Pod、部署和其他工作负载整理为健康状态与集群模型。在面板的 Kubernetes 视图中查看汇总。
DSH Monitor 的功能「仓库与应用概览」：扫描配置目录下的 Git 仓库，并在 macOS 上读取已安装应用及可选的 Homebrew 信息。用户可从系统面板的对应视图查看项目和应用状态。

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · dsh-monitor：A monitoring plugin for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness): machine health, runtime state, the git repositories you work in, and the Kubernetes cluster you develop on — from one sidebar entry, without leaving the app.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · dsh-monitor：The **Système** entry carries four sub-views, switched from the tabs at the top of the panel: **Machine** answers « is this machine healthy? » in one scroll, **Kubernetes** answers « what runs in the cluster, what is degraded, and why? », **Dépôts** answers « what is the state of the git workspace, and what is left to push? », and **Applications** answers « what is installed on this Mac, and what is out of date? ». The four interfaces are written in French.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：- **Machine** — CPU, memory, disk, load average, battery, swap, the top processes and a **Processeur** card that draws the processor over time. A sample is appended to `cpu.jsonl` every 60 s, whether the panel is open or not, and kept for 24 h; the card reads that file back in one of three windows (1 h, 6 h, 24 h — it opens on 1 h), draws the average of each bucket as one curve, says for every point what the average and the peak were over its measures, sums the window up (current, minimum, average, maximum), and explains itself instead of showing a blank plot when the file holds nothing yet. Memory follows the Activity Monitor definition (app + wired + compressed) instead of the naive `total - free`, which sits at ~99 % as soon as the OS keeps inactive pages. CPU is a delta over a real time window on both platforms: a `/proc/stat` sample on Linux, the second `top -l 2 -s 1` sample on macOS. Linux reads `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/stat`, `/proc/swaps` and `/sys/class/power_supply` directly. When Colima is present, its VM disk is measured through `colima ssh -- df -kP` and reported separately from the host disk.
- **DSH** — active sessions,

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：The panel refreshes on open, on window focus, and every 60 s while visible — no background polling. The last snapshot is cached in `localStorage` and painted immediately on the next open.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：`/systeme/api/etat` always answers with the latest snapshot (stale-while-revalidate) and rebuilds in the background, so the panel never blocks on a slow probe. A snapshot is rebuilt at most every 15 s, with per-section caching for the expensive parts (repositories 3 min, pull requests 60 s, runtime 90 s, cluster 20 s, applications 60 s, machine and Colima disk 15 s). Pull requests are read with `gh pr list` when `gh` is installed and authenticated; without it the column stays at « — » and the rest of the view still renders. `?refresh=1` forces a rebuild after a remediation.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：The free-space modal reads `GET /systeme/api/disque` when it opens — `docker system df`, the Colima filesystems, and the size of the `node_modules` and artefact folders of the repositories with no commit in 30 days. That reading takes ten seconds and more (`docker system df` alone costs about seven on a full Docker store), so the modal waits on a loader that names it: the spinner, « Analyse des cibles… », the time it started and the three families it measures, with `aria-busy` on the dialog; the loader goes as soon as the reading lands, and an error takes the plain banner. `Fermer`, the close button and the overlay stay live throughout — the analysis is a read, there is nothing to lock.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：The machine view also exposes `GET /systeme/api/cpu?fenetre=1h|6h|24h`: the stored CPU history reduced to about 120 points over the requested window, each point carrying its average, its peak and how many samples it joins, plus the current, minimum, average and maximum of the window and the path of the file that was read. Any other `fenetre` falls back to `1h`. The file is written by the panel's own sampler — one `{"at","cpu"}` line every 60 s, from the moment the panel starts and whether or not the tab is open — and is rewritten without its expired lines when it is loaded; the snapshot itself no longer carries a CPU history.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：The applications view also exposes `/systeme/api/app?name=<bundle>`, which returns the identifiers, versions on both sides, signature, architecture, size and quarantine of one bundle, each of its sub-bundles, the two commands the panel ran, and a guard against names that leave the scanned folders: the name is resolved against the last snapshot, never against the disk, and an optional `path` picks one of two bundles that share a name. The snapshot is reused, so a drawer costs a handful of `plutil` and `codesign` calls and never a `brew` call.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：The applications view also exposes `GET /systeme/api/app/footprint?name=<bundle>&path=<path>`, the removal inventory: the bundle, the data and configuration the panel attributes to it — each line with its size, and the `nom` tag for a folder named after the app —, the shared group containers and system-wide folders it will not touch, whether the application is running, and whether removal is refused (`system` for a bundle macOS owns, `pkg` for a bundle a package receipt claims, with the `pkgid` in the reason). It is read-only and costs one `du`, one `pkgutil` and one `pgrep`. The removal itself is `POST /systeme/api/action` with `{famille: 'apps', action: 'supprimer', name, path, data, config, confirm: true}`: the server recomputes the inventory and never takes a path from the client, answers 409 for a running application, 422 for a refused bundle or a Finder that was not granted the Automation permission, and returns the journal entry plus a `receipt` (elements, bytes, what the Finder and `brew` handled, what stayed behind).

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：The applications view exposes `GET /systeme/api/homebrew/plan`, the synchronisation plan as the panel would run it: the formulae and the cask tokens that are out of date, the casks set aside with their bundle and recipe versions, and the commands in order. It costs no `brew` call — it reads the snapshot. The gesture itself is `POST /systeme/api/action` with `{famille: 'homebrew', action: 'synchroniser', confirm: true}`: the server rebuilds the plan from its own snapshot, never takes a token from the client, answers 409 when there is nothing to upgrade, and returns the journal entry plus a `receipt` (the plan, one verdict per step with its duration and the tail of its output, the steps that never ran, and the counts left after a fresh reading).

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · What it shows：The repositories view also exposes `/systeme/api/depot?name=<repository>`, which returns the last four commits, the raw `git status --porcelain=v2 --branch` output and the stashes of one repository; the name is restricted to a direct child of `projectsRoot`.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Configuration：The plugin is configured on its `cordis.patch.yml` entry, from a page the package brings to **Plugins → Système**. Saving the page writes the values into the profile patch (the YAML below), so the configuration stays in the profile's own file.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Configuration：The page is split in four sections: **Général** first, with the panel refresh cadence, then **Dépôts git**, **Kubernetes** and **Applications**. The Applications section is only shown on macOS; its first switch hides the tab, its second asks Homebrew (without it the bundle reading still runs). The context picker sits in the header of the Kubernetes view: it lists the contexts `kubectl` declares on the machine, plus an automatic entry, the default, that follows the current context, and writes the choice straight to `k8sContext`. The cluster check asks that context for its version and makes no assumption about the cluster's flavour. Each of those last two opens with a switch that hides the matching tab — the switch only changes what the panel shows, the collection keeps running in the background so the view comes back with its current values when switched on again.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Configuration：| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `projectsRoot` | `~/projects` | Directory holding the git repositories to watch |
| `showRepos` | `true` | Show the Dépôts tab |
| `k8sContext` | `''` | Watched `kubectl` context, chosen from the Kubernetes card of the panel among the contexts the machine detects; empty follows the current context |
| `showK8s` | `true` | Show the Kubernetes sections |
| `showApps` | `true` | Show the Applications tab (macOS only) |
| `showBrew` | `true` | Ask Homebrew when the Applications tab is read — `brew --version`, `brew list`, `brew outdated`; off limits the tab to the bundles |
| `costLedger` | `~/.dsh/storages/cost-meter/ledger.json` | Ledger written by `dsh-cost-meter` (`days.<YYYY-MM-DD>.cost`, `.calls`, `config.currency`/`config.symbol`); empty hides the cost row. Not shown on the page — override it in the YAML only when the ledger lives elsewhere |
| `refreshSeconds` | `60` | Panel refresh cadence, in seconds, clamped between `15` and `900` |

- insert:
    - id: systeme
      name: '@daedalforge/dsh-monitor'
      config:

An empty field clears its key and falls back to the schema default. The panel follows `refreshSeconds` and the two card switches without a restart: they are volatile values, read at each build of the state.

Thresholds are edited from the panel and stored in `~/.dsh/storages/dsh-monitor/config.json`:

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Configuration：| Measure | Attention | Alert |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free disk (host and Colima VM) | < 20 % | < 10 % |
| Memory used | > 80 % | > 90 % |
| Load | > 1 × cores | > 2 × cores |
| Battery | < 20 % | < 10 % |
| Dirty repository | > 3 days | > 7 days |
| Pod restarts | > 2 | > 5 |

Journal: `~/.dsh/storages/dsh-monitor/journal.jsonl`. Last Kubernetes state: `~/.dsh/storages/dsh-monitor/k8s-last.json`. CPU history: `~/.dsh/storages/dsh-monitor/cpu.jsonl`, one sample per 60 s and 24 h of retention.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Remediations：Every action requires a confirmation naming the target and the measured impact. Nothing runs without `confirm: true`; the outcome is written to the journal and the panel refreshes.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Remediations：| Family | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| Process | SIGTERM then SIGKILL after 5 s — PID 1, system processes, the DSH host and container runtimes are protected |
| DSH | Stop a job of the current session, empty `~/.dsh/cache` |
| Disk | Docker prune without volumes, DSH cache, `node_modules` of repositories with no commit in 30 days, `dist/build/.next/target` artifacts of those repositories — never a git-tracked file |
| Kubernetes | `rollout restart` of a deployment, delete a pod, purge a finished job |
@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Remediations：No Docker volume is ever removed, no secret is read, no git write is performed, no automatic remediation runs.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Prerequisites：- DeepSeek Harness `>=0.2.1-rc.5 <0.3.0-0`. The range sits in `engines.dsh`, so a host outside it refuses the plugin rather than loading a panel it was never tested against.
- The app's own Node runtime, 20 or later. Nothing else is installed for the panel to work.
- macOS or Linux. Windows is not supported: the machine collectors branch on `process.platform` and otherwise read procfs.
- Optional tools. Each one enables a part of the panel; without it that part is hidden or reads `—`, never an error:

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Prerequisites：| Tool | Without it |
| --- | --- |
| `gh`, authenticated | pull request columns show `—` |
| `kubectl`, plus `docker` or `colima`, plus `kind` | the `Kubernetes` tab is hidden |
| `git`, with checkouts under `projectsRoot` | the `Dépôts` tab is hidden |

- No configuration file is required: the defaults (`~/projects`, a 60 s refresh, local same-origin requests only) apply as is.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Install：```sh
dsh plugin --profile desktop add @daedalforge/dsh-monitor
```

Restart the application completely (Cmd+Q) — a new server route is not picked up by a client reload.

From a tarball or a git checkout:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile desktop add file:/path/to/daedalforge-dsh-monitor-<version>.tgz
```

Uninstall:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile desktop remove @daedalforge/dsh-monitor
```

Files under `~/.dsh/storages/dsh-monitor/` stay in place; delete them by hand if you want a clean slate.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Architecture：- `lib/index.js` — server side: collectors, thresholds, actions, journal. Routes `/systeme/api/etat`, `/systeme/api/disque`, `/systeme/api/action`, `/systeme/api/journal`, `/systeme/api/reglages`, `/systeme/api/app`, `/systeme/api/app/footprint`, `/systeme/api/cpu`. Requests must be local and same-origin; anything else gets a 403.
- `lib/apps.js` — the macOS reading: the app folders scanned, each bundle's `Info.plist` and signature, the Homebrew formulae and casks, and the join that says whether a cask and its bundle agree. Bounded by one `brew` call batch and a per-bundle `plutil`, and skipped entirely when Homebrew is switched off.
- `lib/k8s.js` — the Kubernetes reading: raw `kubectl` objects in, one model out (counters, capacity, causes, namespace rows, topology, components, activity). Pure and unit-tested, so the panel logic is verified without a live cluster.
- `lib/client.js` — the React panel loaded by the DSH client — `Système`, with its `Machine`, `Kubernetes`, `Dépôts` and `Applications` views — styles scoped under `.dsh-systeme` and `.dsh-kube`.
- `cordis.patch.yml` — inserts the `systeme` entry.
@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：The version is never set by hand. Every push to `main` reads the commits since the last `vX.Y.Z` tag and takes the highest bump their messages ask for:

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：| Commit messages since the last tag | Version |
| --- | --- |
| one starts with `feat:` | minor — `y` plus one, `z` back to zero |
| one carries `!` before the colon (`feat!:`, `fix!:`) or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer | major — `x` plus one, `y` and `z` back to zero |
| anything else (`fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, a plain sentence) | patch — `z` plus one |

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：It writes that version into `package.json` with a commit created through the GitHub API, so GitHub signs it; tags the commit; and opens a GitHub release. The release commit is skipped by the same trigger, so the workflow never loops. With no tag yet, the version sitting in `package.json` is released as is — that is the first release.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：Opening the release is what publishes: a second workflow runs on `release: published`, checks the tag against `package.json`, runs the tests, publishes to npm with provenance, and attaches the tarball to the release. Publishing a release by hand from the GitHub interface therefore works the same way.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：The release workflow writes to `main`, which a branch ruleset guards with a pull request and a verified signature. It does so under a dedicated GitHub App, whose installation token it mints with `actions/create-github-app-token`; that app sits on the bypass list of both rulesets, so the version commit, the tag and the release land without weakening the rules. Two secrets carry the identity: `APP_ID`, and `APP_PRIVATE_KEY` holding the app's private key. The release must be opened with that app token and not with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, or the `Publish` workflow would never run.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：Trusted publishing only adds a version to a package that already exists; it cannot create the package. The very first version therefore has to be pushed by a person holding the npm account, with two-factor authentication enabled — a security key or an authenticator app, which npm asks for in the browser. From the tagged commit:

```sh
npm login
npm publish --access public
```

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：That first version is the only one without provenance. Everything after it goes through the workflow, which authenticates through npm trusted publishing: no token is stored in the repository, the workflow file is the credential.

```sh
npm trust github @daedalforge/dsh-monitor --repo daedalforge/dsh-monitor --file publish.yml --allow-publish
```

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Releases：Run that once the package exists. The trust configuration lives inside the package, so deleting the package deletes it too — including the placeholder npm creates on its own while a staged publish is pending, and removes again when that staged publish is rejected.

A publish that fails can be replayed from the Actions tab, with the tag to publish as input.

@daedalforge/dsh-monitor README · Limits：- Machine metrics use macOS tools (`vm_stat`, `sysctl`, `pmset`, `top`) or procfs/sysfs on Linux; `ps` and `df` are used on both. Kubernetes inspection only needs `kubectl` pointing at a reachable context: liveness is the API's own version endpoint, so no local runtime and no particular cluster flavour is required. The runtime drawn in the topology is the first one found on `PATH` (`docker`, `podman` or `nerdctl`, with `colima` reported when present); the cluster itself is never created, started or stopped by the panel. The plugin reads nodes, pods, deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets, jobs, cronjobs, namespaces, PVCs, services, ingresses and external secrets, plus Warning events, and needs no metrics-server: reservations come from the pod specs, not from measured usage.
- The Applications view reads what macOS and Homebrew expose. App Store applications are out of scope, a bundle pushed by an MDM is read like any other bundle — the panel does not know a management console's version and never compares against one, and it refuses to remove a bundle a package receipt claims rather than pretending to know which console owns it — and only cask
